# setup-refinery v1.0.0

**Run your SQL migrations in CI without waiting for a Rust compiler.**

[refinery](https://github.com/rust-db/refinery) is a great migration tool with one CI-shaped
problem: upstream stopped shipping prebuilt binaries. Releases `v0.9.0`, `v0.9.1` and `v0.9.2` have
**zero release assets** — their release workflow triggers on tags matching `[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+`,
and from 0.9.0 onward their tags gained a `v` prefix, so it never fires again.

That leaves `cargo install refinery_cli`: three to ten minutes of compiling MySQL, Postgres, SQLite
and SQL Server drivers — including SQLite from C source — on **every single run**, billed at 2× on
Windows and 10× on macOS.

This action replaces that with a download.

```yaml
- uses: danielsan/setup-refinery@v1
  with:
    version: '0.9.2'

- run: refinery migrate -e DATABASE_URL -p ./migrations
```

## Measured, not estimated

Timings from the v1.0.0 verification run, on the hosted runners, for the action step itself:

| Runner | Install time |
| --- | --- |
| `ubuntu-latest` (x64) | **1s** |
| `ubuntu-24.04-arm` (arm64) | **1s** |
| `macos-latest` (arm64) | **1s** |
| `windows-latest` (x64) | **3s** |
| `macos-15-intel` (x64) | **7s** |

Five platforms, one `uses:` line. No Docker image to pull, no Rust toolchain to set up, no
`actions/cache` to configure — and nothing to configure at all if you just want the latest version.

## Built to be trusted, not just fast

You are putting a third party's binary on your runner's `PATH`. That deserves more than a shrug:

- **Every download is SHA-256 verified and fails closed.** There is no skip-checksum input and there
  never will be. On a mismatch the action retries the download exactly once, then fails without
  installing anything.
- **Built from crates.io, not a git clone.** The source is the immutable, content-addressed `.crate`
  tarball, and its sha256 is checked against the crates.io API before a single line compiles.
- **Build provenance attestations** ([`actions/attest-build-provenance`]) — verify any asset with
  `gh attestation verify`.
- **A release is all-or-nothing.** If any one of the five targets fails to build, verify, or upload,
  nothing is published. You can never resolve `latest` onto a half-populated release.
- **The real action is smoke-tested on all five runner platforms before publication**, downloading
  over the public path with a read-only token — the same path your workflow takes.
- **Every archive carries `BUILDINFO.txt`**: the upstream commit, the `.crate` sha256, the binary's
  own sha256, `rustc -vV`, the exact cargo invocation, the enabled features, and the exact delta
  from a vanilla `cargo install`. Nothing about how these binaries were made is a mystery.
- **Linux binaries are static musl**, so they run on Alpine and on any glibc vintage. No
  `GLIBC_2.34 not found`.

[`actions/attest-build-provenance`]: https://github.com/actions/attest-build-provenance

## What's compiled in

Upstream's default features: **`mysql`**, **`postgresql`**, **`sqlite-bundled`**, **`mssql`** — all
four drivers in one binary. SQLite is bundled and built with `SQLITE_ENABLE_MATH_FUNCTIONS`, and the
release profile settings are replicated, both matching upstream's own workspace.

Three things worth knowing before you pin a version, because they are easy to discover the hard way:

- **`int8-versions` is OFF.** Migration versions are `i32` and `refinery_schema_history` keeps its
  standard semantics. A `--all-features` build — including upstream's own release workflow — differs
  here.
- **Postgres TLS needs 0.9.2 or later.** Upstream 0.9.0 and 0.9.1 map the `postgresql` feature to a
  driver with no TLS backend at all, so `?sslmode=require` cannot work on those binaries regardless
  of configuration. If you are connecting to RDS, Cloud SQL, Supabase or Neon, use 0.9.2. We publish
  0.9.0 and 0.9.1 for completeness and label it in their `BUILDINFO.txt` and notices.
- **MSSQL connections are not encrypted** and Windows integrated auth is unavailable: upstream
  builds `tiberius` with `default-features = false`. That is upstream's choice, not ours, but you
  should know it before pointing this at a SQL Server.

## Refinery versions available

`0.9.2`, `0.9.1`, `0.9.0` — the entire 0.9 line upstream never published. Ask for an exact version
(`0.9.2`), a partial one (`0.9` → newest 0.9.x), or `latest`.

**Pinning is free and worth it.** An exact version makes **zero API calls** — the asset URL is
deterministic, so a pinned workflow cannot be rate-limited, ever. New refinery releases are picked
up automatically by a daily crates.io poll, so `version: latest` on `@v1` keeps working without you
updating anything.

## Inputs

Three, and they are a deliberate commitment to stay that way.

| Input | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `version` | `latest` | `latest`, exact (`0.9.2`), or partial (`0.9`) |
| `token` | `${{ github.token }}` | Only used to resolve `latest`/partial. Defaulted so rate limits never reach you |
| `fallback` | `none` | Set to `cargo` to build from source when no prebuilt asset exists |

Outputs: `version`, `bin-path`, `cache-hit`.

## Scope

This action **installs** refinery and gets out of the way. It does not run your migrations for you —
you call `refinery migrate` yourself, with your own flags, in your own step, and you keep the full
CLI rather than whatever subset an action's inputs happen to expose.

## Working with a coding agent?

[`docs/for-coding-agents.md`](../../docs/for-coding-agents.md) is written for Claude, Copilot, Cursor
and friends: the two-step answer, the five mistakes agents actually make, the **verified** migration
filename rules (which filenames are silently ignored versus which abort the whole run), and a
paste-ready block for your own `AGENTS.md`.
